reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Caused by infarction of the medial medulla, usually from occlusion of paramedian branches of the anterior spinal artery or the distal vertebral artery
Presents as a classic crossed picture: contralateral limb weakness with ipsilateral tongue deviation
Contralateral hemiparesis spares the face because the lesion lies below the facial nucleus and affects the pyramid
Ipsilateral tongue wasting and deviation towards the weak side reflect hypoglossal nerve involvement
Contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration follows medial lemniscus involvement, while pain and temperature are typically preserved
Bilateral medial medullary infarction is rare but can cause quadriparesis and mimic more caudal spinal cord disease
Upbeat nystagmus may occur from involvement of medial longitudinal fasciculus fibres near the midline
reference.pathophysiology: Medial medullary infarction results from ischaemia in the paramedian territory supplied by penetrating branches of the anterior spinal artery and distal vertebral artery. Three vertically oriented midline structures are affected: the pyramid carrying the corticospinal tract (contralateral limb weakness with facial sparing), the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of dorsal-column sensation), and the emerging hypoglossal nerve fibres and nucleus (ipsilateral tongue weakness with deviation to the paretic side). Because the spinothalamic tract and the lateral medullary structures lie outside this territory, pain and temperature sensation and cranial nerves nine and ten are generally spared, giving the characteristic dissociated, crossed deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior spinal artery syndrome of the cervical cord
Demyelinating brainstem lesion in multiple sclerosis
Motor neurone disease with bulbar involvement
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI showing a paramedian medullary infarct, sometimes with a heart-shaped appearance
MR or CT angiography of the vertebral and anterior spinal circulation
Assessment of tongue movement, articulation, and swallowing safety
Vessel wall imaging when dissection or atherosclerosis is suspected
Cardiovascular risk workup including ECG, echocardiography where indicated, and metabolic profiling
Somatosensory testing to document dorsal-column involvement
redFlags: Bilateral involvement producing quadriparesis and respiratory compromise
Rostral extension towards the pons threatening consciousness and airway
Vertebral dissection with risk of recurrent posterior circulation embolism
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an evolving basilar territory event
reference.prognosis: Unilateral cases often show meaningful motor recovery with rehabilitation, but bilateral or extensive infarcts causing quadriparesis and bulbar failure carry a substantially worse outcome.
pitfalls: Confusing the facial-sparing hemiparesis with a hemispheric stroke and misdirecting imaging
Overlooking ipsilateral tongue deviation that localises the lesion to the medial medulla
Missing evolving bilateral infarction that can precipitate respiratory failure
Assuming intact pain and temperature sensation excludes a brainstem stroke
